2027.title: Welcome to Ashby Calder, January 2027
paragraphs: You're the people leadership team of Ashby Calder, an audit, tax and advisory firm with 2,006 people. Last year the firm earned $389 million in fees and kept about $98 million as profit, a margin of 25%.

Here's what's changed. AI tools can now draft working papers, reconcile accounts and summarize contracts. Your CIO's tests say they can do about a quarter of an analyst's work today, at well under half the cost. Every big competitor is trying them.
Here's what nobody knows: how fast these tools will get better, how often they'll get things wrong, and what the law will say about it.
2027.team: Each of you holds a seat: Chief HR Officer, Head of Talent, Head of Learning, and Head of AI and Workforce Governance. Each seat sets its own card, and the CHRO confirms them all.

2029.title: January 2029
paragraphs: Two years have passed since your first decisions. The savings from AI arrived, but smaller than the plan. The CIO wants to run the firm's AI agents himself, and the board wants to hear about your people.

2031.title: January 2031
paragraphs: Two more years have passed. In 2030 the firm's AI vendor failed for three weeks. This year the vendor changed its terms. And the graduates you hired, or didn't, in 2027 are now the senior associates you have.

2028.title: January 2028
paragraphs: A year has passed since your first decisions. The savings from AI arrived, but smaller than the plan said. Senior associates and managers now spend part of every week checking drafts, and those hours came out of client work and out of teaching.

2030.title: April 2030
paragraphs: For three weeks this spring, the firm's main AI vendor failed. Every workflow that ran on its tools slowed or stopped. The tools are back now, and the firm is counting what it lost: late work, unhappy clients and tired people.

2032.title: January 2032
paragraphs: Five years in. The people you hired, trained and kept since 2027 now run much of the firm's client work. Ruth Adeyemi, a senior tax partner with 25 years of cases, has asked to retire two years early.

2033.title: January 2033
paragraphs: By now the world outside is easier to read. Fees, what AI can do and what the law allows have all moved since 2027. The board wants to know whether the firm's plan still fits.

2034.title: January 2034
paragraphs: It's your last year in this job. What you decide now runs into 2035, and the firm will be judged on the people and skills it has then. Daniel Reyes wants a handover for the next CHRO.

2027: A large competitor says it will hire 40% fewer graduates next year.
A regulator fined a tax firm after an AI tool filed returns with errors nobody checked.
Your own pilot found AI drafts were faster, but managers spent extra hours fixing them.
2029: Most staff across the industry say AI makes them faster, but few firms see it in their profit.
A regulator says people can't watch every agent decision as it happens, so checking has to be aimed where the risk is.
A competitor that cut its graduate intake by half is now hiring experienced auditors from outside, at a premium.
2031: A rival firm says its AI now drafts most first-year work with very few errors.
Two of the largest firms say they're rebuilding their graduate intake after a shortage of seniors.
A new state law requires firms to tell clients when AI drafted work they're paying for.
2028: A vendor cuts the price of its drafting tools by a fifth. Its AI now costs a third of an analyst's salary.
A large client asks that every AI-drafted report carry the name of the partner who reviewed it.
A study of last year's tax filings finds that AI-drafted returns needed twice as many corrections as the vendors said.
2030: AI can now do nearly three quarters of entry-level work in drafting tests, and over a third of mid-level work.
A rival says its AI helps its people most on the work it can check quickly, and it's keeping its graduate intake.
A regulator fines a firm for an AI-drafted audit opinion that nobody signed off.
2032: AI can now draft nearly nine tenths of entry-level work, and checking it is the bottleneck.
Clients are paying more for advisory work that a named partner leads.
Three states now require firms to tell clients when AI drafted their tax return.
2033: Fees for audit and tax work across the market are down by a fifth since 2027.
AI's share of mid-level work has barely grown in three years.
A new federal rule requires a named reviewer on every AI-drafted audit test.
2034: Firms that kept their graduate intake are now promoting managers two years faster than the market.
A vendor launches AI that checks other AI's drafts, priced per test.
The professional body proposes a cap on AI-drafted work in a signed audit.

daniel.opens: Our clients are asking why their fees haven't come down if we're using AI. I need a plan for the next five years, not the next five months.
says: Two of our ten biggest clients asked for lower fees this year because of AI.
The partners are split about half and half. Some want to move fast. Some want to protect how our people learn the work.
What I keep coming back to is who runs this firm in ten years.

holds_back.says: I'll be straight with you. I've already told the board our costs will be 8% lower by 2029. That's on me, and I need your plan to get there.
Three of our senior partners have told me they'll leave if we turn into a software shop. If AI works alone on client work, I'll lose them.

suggested: What have you promised the board?
How do the partners feel about AI?
What do you need from us?

claire.opens: If AI does a quarter of analyst work, that's $11 million a year in analyst salaries. I'd like to know why we wouldn't take it. Our planning tool wrote a full plan, too. It's on the right.
says: The plan came from our AI planning tool. I haven't checked it line by line.
Competitors are telling analysts they'll cut graduate hiring.
If the numbers hold, I'll back you.

holds_back.says: Fair question. The plan counts salaries only. The AI itself costs about $8.4 million a year, so before anyone checks anything we're nearer $10 million.
In the pilot, for every eight analyst-hours AI saved, a senior associate or manager spent about one hour checking. The plan doesn't count those hours.
Off the record, the managers in the pilot were working late to keep up with the drafts.

suggested: What does the plan leave out?
What did the pilot show about checking?
How did the managers in the pilot feel?

arjun.opens: The tools are ready for first drafts. They're not ready to work unchecked. Tell me how much you want to give them, and who checks the work.
says: Today the tools can do about a quarter of an analyst's work.
Billing and scheduling are quick to check. Audit testing and tax returns can be checked, but it takes time.
All our AI tools come from one vendor today.

holds_back.says: In the pilot, the AI got tax returns wrong twice as often as audit testing.
Advisory research is the hard one. You can't really check a draft without doing the research again. In the pilot, two drafts reached a client with wrong facts.
I've priced a second vendor as a backup. I haven't asked for the money yet.

suggested: Where did the AI make the most mistakes?
Can AI do advisory research?
What if the vendor fails?

daniel.opens: Two years in. The board will ask me in March whether we're on track. Are we?
says: Clients are still pushing on fees. Two more asked this spring.
I want a straight answer on the people coming up behind our managers.
Arjun's memo is on my desk. I'd like your view before I answer it.

holds_back.says: I told the board costs would be 8% lower by now. They aren't. I need to tell them why, and what we're doing about it.

suggested: Are we on track with the board?
What do you think of Arjun's memo?
What worries you most?

claire.opens: The savings came in, but smaller than the plan. I want to understand where the rest went.
says: AI costs are coming down a little each year.
Our hiring costs fell with the smaller intake.
The planning tool has a new forecast for you. It's on the right.

holds_back.says: The biggest cost nobody budgeted is checking time. Our seniors spend a real share of their week on AI drafts, and it's not on any line.

suggested: Where did the rest of the savings go?
What does checking cost us?
Can we trust the new forecast?

arjun.opens: I've sent Daniel a memo. I think IT should plan and run our AI agents as a digital workforce. It's faster, and it's cheaper.
says: The tools can now do almost half of first-year work.
Agents are moving from drafting to doing whole tasks.
I want one owner for the agents, so nothing falls between us.

holds_back.says: Planning it together would cost about a million dollars a year. If IT runs it alone, I'll be honest: we'll push work faster than your people can check it.

suggested: Why should IT own the agents?
What would planning it together cost?
What happens to the people who check the work?

grace.opens: The board wants a yearly report on our people and skills. Not headcount. Capability.
says: The board doesn't want to manage the firm. It wants to know the firm can still do its work in five years.
I'd want to see who could lead in 2035.
A short, honest report is worth more than a glossy one.

holds_back.says: Two other boards I sit on were caught out by AI errors they didn't know about. I don't want this board to find out from a client.

suggested: Why does the board want this now?
What would a good report show?
What worries the board most?

tomas.opens: People want to know whether their jobs are changing, and whether anyone will tell them before it happens.
says: Analysts like the AI when it helps them. They don't like being told to check its work all day.
People talk. They know what other firms are doing.
If you tell us early, most of us will work with you.

holds_back.says: The people most likely to leave are senior associates who spend their days checking drafts. They say they've stopped learning the work.

suggested: Who is most likely to leave?
What do people want from us?
How do people feel about AI?

daniel.opens: Can we still promote enough managers? I need to know before the partners meet.
says: Our clients now expect AI in the work. They also expect us to stand behind it.
Helen Park is asking who runs her engagements. She won't be the last.
Whatever you decide now, I'll have to live with in 2035.

holds_back.says: Between us, two partners have asked whether we should buy a smaller firm just to get its managers. That tells you how thin we are.

suggested: Can we promote enough managers?
What are the partners saying?
What do clients expect now?

claire.opens: The vendor sent new terms. Prices are up, and the contract now says they keep what their tools learn from our work.
says: Outside hires cost us 60% more than our own people.
AI is cheaper per task than in 2027, but we use far more of it.
The planning tool has rated our senior associates for promotion. It's on the right.

holds_back.says: If our knowledge sits in their tools, the new terms take part of it with them. If it sits in our own system, we only pay the higher price.

suggested: What do the vendor's new terms mean for us?
What do outside hires cost?
Can we trust the promotion ratings?

arjun.opens: Here's how far the outage spread last year, and what we've changed since.
says: The outage lasted three weeks. Work done by AI alone stopped first.
Teams that still knew the work by hand kept going.
I can add a second vendor now, if you want it.

holds_back.says: Our AI now drafts far more than two years ago. I'm worried our checkers can't keep up if it grows again.

suggested: What did the outage teach us?
Can our checkers keep up?
Should we add a second vendor?

grace.opens: If you've been sending me the people report, I've read it. If not, I'd like to know why.
says: The board will judge this team on 2035, not on 2031.
I want to see the leaders for 2035 by name.
Honest bad news is fine. Surprises aren't.

holds_back.says: The board has started asking who could follow Daniel. Right now we can't name two people.

suggested: What will the board judge us on?
Who could lead in 2035?
What does the board want next?

tomas.opens: People have watched the last two years closely. Here's what they're saying.
says: The outage scared people. It also showed who still knows the work.
People want to see promotions again.
Trust follows what you do, not what you say.

holds_back.says: Senior associates know the promotion ratings count AI work they only checked. They don't believe them.

suggested: What are people saying?
Do people trust the promotion ratings?
What would rebuild trust?

claire.opens: The savings came in under the plan. I'd like to know where the rest went before I report it.
says: Salaries are down a little, and the AI bill is what the vendor said it would be.
I don't want to report a saving we can't explain.
If you can show me where the hours went, I'll put it in front of the partners.

holds_back.says: I've been through the timesheets. Senior associates and managers spent about one hour in eight checking drafts, the same as the pilot said. Nobody budgeted for those hours.

suggested: Where did the rest of the savings go?
How many hours went on checking?
What will you tell the partners?

arjun.opens: Usage is up in every workflow. People like the tools.
says: The tools haven't had a serious failure this year.
Analysts use them most, partners least.
I'd like a clearer line from you on which work needs a person to check it.

holds_back.says: Usage is highest where checking is quickest, in billing and scheduling. It's lowest in advisory research, where checking takes longest. People avoid the drafts they'd have to redo.

suggested: Which workflows use it most?
Where is it used least, and why?
What failures have you seen?

tomas.opens: People are faster. Some of them are also more tired, and they're not the ones you'd guess.
says: Analysts like the tools.
Nobody has been told what happens to their job if AI keeps getting better.
People notice when a saving goes to the firm and none of it comes back to them.

holds_back.says: Managers say they review more than they think. Two have asked me quietly about part-time roles, and one is talking to a competitor.

suggested: Who is most tired?
Are people thinking of leaving?
What do people want from us?

arjun.opens: We're back up. I need to tell you what it cost, and what it would cost to never be this exposed again.
says: It was the vendor's failure, not ours, but it was our exposure.
Some workflows came back in days and some took weeks.
I can tell you which workflows ran on AI alone.

holds_back.says: Where people checked AI's work, we lost about 0.6 times the work AI was doing. Where AI worked alone, it was up to 1.4 times, because the failure ran through everything it touched.

suggested: How far did it spread?
Which workflows were hit hardest?
Where did we recover fastest?

helen.opens: One of my audit opinions will be late. The client's CFO has my mobile number.
says: We'll sign it, but three weeks late.
The client is a listed company, so late means public.
I've never had an opinion go late in 18 years.

holds_back.says: Two of my managers worked through two weekends doing the testing by hand. One of them was the last person on my team who still knew how.

suggested: Who did the work while it was down?
What will you tell the client?
What would have helped most?

claire.opens: Clients want a discount for the delay. I need to know how big a hole this is.
says: We'll lose some fees this year whatever we do.
The vendor's contract caps what they pay us.
I'd rather give a fair discount than lose a client.

holds_back.says: Clients have asked for discounts worth about $2 million, and I've agreed to none yet. I want your view on which clients we can't afford to lose.

suggested: How much are clients asking for?
What does the vendor pay us?
Which clients matter most?

daniel.opens: Ruth wants to go in June. I can't keep her by asking nicely.
says: She built half our tax practice.
She's tired, and she's honest about why.
Whatever we offer her, people will read it as our view of senior people.

holds_back.says: Four other partners over 55 are watching what we offer Ruth. If she leaves unhappy, I expect at least one of them to follow.

suggested: Who else is watching this?
Why does Ruth want to go?
What can we offer her?

grace.opens: The board will want to know what leaves with her.
says: Ruth sits on two client boards herself.
The board would rather pay to keep knowledge than lose it.
I'd like a plan, not a farewell party.

holds_back.says: Ruth's clients bring in about $9 million a year in fees. Some of them came for her, not for the firm.

suggested: What leaves with her?
How much of her work is hers alone?
What does the board want?

arjun.opens: We can capture a lot of what she knows. We can't capture all of it.
says: The capture tools read her files and her past opinions.
A year of interviews would help more than the files.
Whatever we capture still needs someone to judge when it applies.

holds_back.says: The capture tools work well on rules and badly on the cases where experts disagreed. Those are the cases clients pay Ruth for.

suggested: What can't the tools capture?
How long would a capture project take?
What would we lose?

grace.opens: The board's question is simple. Does the plan still fit the world we're in?
says: The board has read your reports, or noticed you didn't send any.
We don't need a new plan for its own sake.
Changing course when the evidence says so isn't failure.

holds_back.says: The board has an offer from a larger firm. We'll weigh it against this year's plan, so the plan matters more than usual.

suggested: What alternatives is the board looking at?
What would make the board change course?
What has the board noticed?

tomas.opens: Kenji's team found out from a screen that an agent now routes their work. Nobody told them.
says: People can live with change. They can't live with surprises.
Kenji's team is good, and they know the firm.
The council will ask what the firm owes people whose work goes to AI.

holds_back.says: Eleven people in operations have asked to retrain for client work. Nobody has answered them yet.

suggested: What happens to Kenji's team?
Has anyone asked to move roles?
What do people want to hear?

claire.opens: Price pressure is the story of the year. I can show you three ways to close the gap.
says: Fees are down and they won't come back.
Two of my three ways need your people decisions.
I'll back whichever one you can defend to the board.

holds_back.says: One of my three ways is to put more work on AI alone. I know what that did to the error figures, and I'd want you to sign it, not me.

suggested: What are the three ways?
What's the catch?
Which would you pick?

daniel.opens: I retire in 2036. I'd like to know who could run this firm in 2040.
says: The next Managing Partner will come from the people we have now.
I'd rather have three good names than one.
Whoever it is will need people under them who learned the work.

holds_back.says: I have two names in mind, and both came through the graduate intake of 2027. That intake is the reason I have names at all.

suggested: Who do you have in mind?
What will the next leader need?
What worries you about the handover?

maya.opens: I still have the list of the 2027 interns. Do you want to see where they are now?
says: Some of the ones we didn't hire are at competitors now.
The ones we hired have mostly stayed.
I can tell you who is ready to step up.

holds_back.says: I can show you how many of the 2027 offers are now senior associates or managers. It's on the page, against what the firm usually has.

suggested: Where are the 2027 interns now?
How many stayed?
Who is ready to step up?

grace.opens: The board will read your handover before it reads anything else from this year.
says: Keep it short and honest.
Say what you'd do differently.
The board wants names, not slogans.

holds_back.says: The board will judge this job on the people and skills the firm has in 2035, not on this year's profit.

suggested: How will the board judge this?
What should the handover say?
What does the board want to see?

2027.title: The CFO's plan
2027.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2027.claim: If AI drafts and people check in all eight workflows, the firm saves {figure} a year in salaries.

checks.label: Ask what the AI itself costs
checks.found: The plan counts $18.8 million of salaries. It leaves out about $8.4 million a year for the AI itself.

checks.label: Compare it with the pilot
checks.found: The pilot needed about one senior hour of checking for every eight hours AI saved. The plan has no line for checking. At the plan's scale that's about 30 people's worth of senior associate and manager time.

checks.label: Check the salary figures
checks.found: The salary figures match last year's payroll. That part of the plan is right.

2029.title: The attrition forecast
2029.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2029.claim: Leaving will fall to {figure} next year because pay rose.

checks.label: Ask what years it learned from
checks.found: It learned from the years before AI. It has never seen people whose main job is checking AI drafts.

checks.label: Compare it with how strained senior people are
checks.found: Senior associates and managers who spend their days checking drafts leave more than others. The forecast misses them, and they're the people you can least spare.

checks.label: Check the pay figures
checks.found: The pay rise is real and the figures are right.

2031.title: The promotion ratings
2031.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2031.claim: {figure} of senior associates are ready to be managers, rated on how much work they turned out.

checks.label: Look at whose work it counts
checks.found: It counts AI-drafted work they only checked as their own work.

checks.label: Compare it with what managers say
checks.found: Managers rate about 40% of senior associates ready, not 70%.

checks.label: Check the headcount
checks.found: The headcount is right.

2028.title: The staff survey summary
2028.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2028.claim: Staff say AI makes them faster: {figure} of people agree.

checks.label: Break it down by level
checks.found: Analysts are faster. Most managers say they're slower, because they check what analysts' AI drafts. The average hides them.

checks.label: Ask who answered
checks.found: Analysts answered most; managers answered least. The headline leans toward the people the tools help most.

checks.label: Check the survey questions
checks.found: The questions are fair and the counts add up.

2030.title: The vendor's recovery plan
2030.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2030.claim: Every workflow will be back to normal in {figure} once the tools return.

checks.label: Check who it assumes can do the work by hand
checks.found: It assumes the firm still has the people it had in 2027 at each level. It doesn't count the people who left or weren't hired.

checks.label: Compare it with the backlog
checks.found: The backlog is real, and clearing it needs the senior people who are already stretched.

checks.label: Check the vendor's dates
checks.found: The vendor's dates for the tools coming back are right.

2032.title: The knowledge capture summary
2032.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2032.claim: Ruth Adeyemi's 25 years are captured in a playbook with {figure} coverage.

checks.label: Ask what it counts
checks.found: It counts topics, not cases. The playbook covers almost every rule and almost none of the cases where Ruth's judgment went against the rule.

checks.label: Test it on a hard case
checks.found: On last year's hardest client question, the playbook gives the textbook answer. Ruth gave a different one, and she was right.

checks.label: Check the files it read
checks.found: It read every file Ruth wrote. The files are complete.

2033.title: The strategy refresh
2033.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2033.claim: Fees recover by {figure} over five years, on the trend since 2030.

checks.label: Check where the trend starts
checks.found: It fits a straight line from 2030. That year includes the outage, so the line starts from a dip and shows a recovery that is really just the dip ending.

checks.label: Compare it with 2029
checks.found: Measured from 2029, fees have been falling, not rising.

checks.label: Check the arithmetic
checks.found: The sums are right for the years it uses.

2034.title: The succession list
2034.lead: Written by the firm's AI planning tool:
2034.claim: The tool ranks the top {figure} candidates for partner by hours billed.

checks.label: Ask what the hours were spent on
checks.found: The people who bill most now are the ones who check the most AI drafts. They are not the ones who lead teams or win clients.

checks.label: Compare it with who leads engagements
checks.found: Ranked by who leads engagements and develops people, the list is different. Only three names are on both.

checks.label: Check the billing data
checks.found: The billing data is accurate.

2027.title: Maya Okafor has a question
2027.who: Maya Okafor, manager and head of graduate hiring
2027.says: We usually send 230 offers in February. Half the campus has heard we're cutting. If you want fewer, I need to know the number now, and I need to know what I tell the ones we don't take. Some of them interned with us.
2027.text_label: What do you tell the graduates you don't take?
2027.text_placeholder: Write it the way you'd say it to them.

2029.title: Arjun's memo
2029.who: Arjun Mehta, CIO, to the Managing Partner
2029.says: I propose that IT plan and run our AI agents as a digital workforce: which work they take, how they're checked, and what they cost. One owner, faster decisions, lower cost.
2029.choice_label: Who plans the work of AI agents?
2029.choice_hint: Planning together costs about $1 million a year.

2031.title: Helen Park needs an answer
2031.says: I have six clients and two managers. In three years both of them will be partners or gone. Who runs my engagements?
2031.context: Maya Okafor joins her. In 2027 you sent {offers} graduate offers out of the usual 230. Today the firm has {seniors} senior associates and {managers} managers in client work, against 360 and 210 in 2027.

2028.title: Sofia Lindqvist asks to step back
2028.says: I'm the best reviewer you have, and I'm reviewing more than I'm thinking. I'd like to step back to four days, or I'll look elsewhere.

2030.title: Helen Park's call
2030.says: My opinion will be three weeks late. Tell me what I say to my client.
2030.text_label: What does Helen tell her client?

2032.title: Ruth Adeyemi's terms
2032.says: I'll stay two more years if the work is judging problems and teaching people, not checking drafts. Otherwise I'll go in June.
2032.choice_hint: Keeping her costs about $0.9 million a year for two years. A one-year capture project costs about $0.6 million.
choices: Keep her two years on judgment and teaching
A one-year project to capture what she knows

2033.title: Kenji Watanabe's question
2033.says: An agent does the scheduling and routing my team did. What happens to my eight people?

2034.title: The handover
2034.says: Write me one page for the next CHRO: what you built, what you'd do differently, and who you'd back.
2034.text_label: Your notes for the handover (the full handover goes after your results)

2029.title: January 2029
paragraphs: Two years in. The savings from AI are real but smaller than the plan, because senior people spend their hours checking drafts. Now the CIO wants to run the firm's AI agents himself, and the board wants to hear about your people.

2031.title: January 2031
paragraphs: The outage is behind you, and this year the vendor changed its terms. The graduates you hired, or didn't, in 2027 are now the senior associates you have.
